title: The history of rust
tagline: From a pillar in Delhi that hardly rusts to a global bill of trillions, people have learned that rust is a small battery.
intro: People have fought rust for about two thousand years, long before they knew what it was. Batteries and ships' hulls turned it into a question of chemistry, then electricity. Today we know how it works and what it costs, and we can use that to protect metal.

eras.name: Old iron, old tricks
eras.summary: Coatings and clever iron that lasted, with no theory behind them.

eras.name: Ships, batteries and sacrifice
eras.summary: Copper hulls, the first battery and the idea of a metal that sacrifices itself.

eras.name: Rust becomes a science
eras.summary: Paint, stainless steel and weathering steel, and a theory of how rust works.

eras.name: Counting the bill
eras.summary: Cost studies, a new look at old iron, and the microbes at work on a wreck.

events.title: Pliny writes down how to keep iron from rusting
events.text: In Book 34 of his Natural History, Pliny notes that iron can be shielded from rust with lead compounds, gypsum and a plant pitch. He says the Greeks called rust antipathia, and he repeats a story that a religious rite could keep a chain at Zeugma from rusting.
events.why: It is one of the oldest written records of paint-like coatings used to keep iron from rusting.

events.title: The Iron Pillar of Delhi is raised
events.where: Delhi, India (first set up elsewhere, probably Udayagiri)
events.text: A pillar of forge-welded wrought iron, about 7 metres tall, was made in the Gupta period and is linked to the king Chandragupta II. It has stood in the weather for about 1,600 years with little rust, and today it stands near New Delhi.
events.why: It showed that iron can last for centuries, and later study showed how.

events.title: Zinc-coated iron on Indian armour
events.text: Pieces of Indian armour in the Royal Armouries collection in the UK are coated with zinc over iron. Inscriptions on them date them to before the 1680s.
events.why: It is among the earliest known cases of zinc used on iron, long before galvanising had a name.

events.title: A Royal Navy ship gets a copper hull
events.text: HMS Alarm was the first Royal Navy ship with a fully copper-sheathed hull. The copper kept out worms and weed. Years later the iron nails that held it on were found badly rotted, because iron touching copper in seawater corrodes fast.
events.why: It was an early, costly lesson in galvanic corrosion, the same effect that makes iron rust faster beside copper.

events.title: Elizabeth Fulhame says water takes part in oxidation
events.text: In An Essay on Combustion, Fulhame argued that many oxidation reactions only happen when water is present, and that water is used and then given back. She also reduced metal salts to metals in water at room temperature.
events.why: Rust, too, needs water, and her work was an early step toward seeing oxidation as chemistry in solution.

events.title: Volta describes the first battery
events.text: Volta wrote to Joseph Banks of the Royal Society about a pile of different metals that gave a steady electric current. The letter was printed in the Philosophical Transactions that year.
events.why: A steady current opened electrochemistry, and a rusting drop is a small battery too.

events.title: The Navy Board asks Humphry Davy about copper hulls
events.text: The Navy Board asked Davy, then President of the Royal Society, to advise on the corrosion of the copper sheets on Royal Navy ships. He began work on it himself in 1823.
events.why: A government problem about ships' hulls brought one of the best chemists of the day to corrosion.

events.title: Davy shows that a sacrificial metal can protect copper
events.text: In a paper read to the Royal Society, Davy reported tests of tin, zinc and iron as protectors for ships' copper. Tin stopped working once a chloride film formed on it, while zinc and iron kept working, and iron was cheaper. A small area of the protector was enough to keep the copper clean.
events.why: It is the first clear case of cathodic protection, the idea behind sacrificial anodes today.

events.title: The Admiralty ends the copper-protector project
events.text: Iron protectors kept the copper bright, but some ships with too many of them grew weed and barnacles. On 19 July 1825 the Admiralty told the Navy Board to stop the project, about two years after it began.
events.why: Protection worked chemically, but the cure had side effects, and engineers had to balance them.

events.title: Faraday proposes the words anode and cathode
events.text: Faraday, who had helped Davy with his experiments, proposed the words cathode and anode in his 1834 paper on electrochemistry. Davy's protecting metals are now called anodes.
events.why: Corrosion science still describes rusting in his words: anode, cathode, electrolyte.

events.title: Sorel patents a way to coat iron with zinc
events.text: Sorel patented a method of protecting iron from rust by dipping it in molten zinc or by coating it with a zinc-based paint. It was a forerunner of modern hot-dip galvanising. Sources give slightly different days in 1837, and zinc dipping was known earlier.
events.why: Zinc coatings became the most common way to protect steel, and they sacrifice themselves if scratched.

events.title: The Eiffel Tower gets its first coat of paint
events.text: The tower was first painted with four coats of Venetian red lead paint. Since then it has been repainted about every seven years on average, 19 times in 130 years, with a twentieth campaign starting in 2019. Each campaign takes about 16 months.
events.why: It shows that painting is a repeating job: a barrier works only while it is whole.

events.title: Edison tries a powered system on ships
events.text: Thomas Edison tried to protect ships with an applied current. It failed, because there was no suitable power source or long-lasting anode material.
events.why: The idea of pushing current into the steel was sound, and it came back once better parts existed.

events.title: Brearley makes the first true stainless steel
events.text: Working at the Brown-Firth research laboratory, Brearley found that adding chromium to iron made a metal that did not rust. He had tried low-carbon steels with about 12 percent chromium in 1912. The first true stainless steel, with 0.24 percent carbon and 12.8 percent chromium, was made on 13 August 1913. He first called it rustless steel.
events.why: Chromium makes a thin, tight oxide film that seals the surface, so an alloy can protect itself.

events.title: Ulick Evans publishes The Corrosion of Metals
events.text: Evans's book was the first textbook to explain the mechanisms of corrosion in a thorough way, with a focus on its electrochemical nature. It was soon translated into German, French and Russian. He later became known as a father of the modern science of corrosion.
events.why: It set out rusting as a small electrochemical cell, the picture this box uses.

events.title: U.S. Steel patents the steel that rusts into a shield
events.text: U.S. Steel commercialised a steel containing small amounts of copper and other elements, first for railway hopper cars. Its corrosion resistance was noticed soon after, and the company named it Cor-Ten.
events.why: It showed that a controlled rust layer can protect, if the alloy is right and the metal can dry between rains.

events.title: An early U.S. estimate of what corrosion costs
events.text: A table of U.S. studies lists an estimate for 1949 of $5.5 billion, which is 2.1 percent of gross national product. The author is not named in the source I used.
events.why: It is the start of a long series of efforts to put a price on rust.

events.title: Weathering steel goes into bridges and buildings
events.text: The Moorestown Interchange over the New Jersey Turnpike (1964) is believed to be the first highway structure in weathering steel. The John Deere headquarters in Moline, Illinois, finished the same year, is believed to be the first building to use it as an architectural material.
events.why: Steel was left bare on purpose and trusted to protect itself.

events.title: A U.S. estimate of $70 billion a year
events.text: A table of U.S. studies lists an estimate for 1975 of $70 billion, which is 4.2 percent of gross national product. Different studies used different methods, so the figures are not directly comparable.
events.why: It showed the bill was large and growing, and set the stage for the 2002 study.

events.title: Balasubramaniam explains why the Delhi pillar resists rust
events.text: Balasubramaniam analysed rust from the pillar and found a thin layer of misawite (a form of iron oxyhydroxide) and a layer of iron phosphate, helped along by the high phosphorus in the iron. The pillar rusted quickly at first, for about three years, and then very little.
events.why: The old smiths' iron was not magic: a particular kind of rust seals the surface, which links to weathering steel.

events.title: The U.S. counts the cost of corrosion
events.who: Koch and colleagues, with the FHWA and NACE
events.text: A federal study estimated the direct cost of corrosion in the United States at $276 billion a year, which is 3.1 percent of GDP. It was widely used as a template for later studies.
events.why: It made a plain figure that governments could act on.

events.title: A rust-eating bacterium is named from the Titanic
events.who: Henrietta Mann, Bhavleen Kaur and colleagues
events.where: Dalhousie University, Canada, and University of Seville, Spain
events.text: Researchers isolated a new bacterium, Halomonas titanicae, from a rusticle on the Titanic wreck about 3.8 kilometres down. In the lab it attached to steel and formed knobs of corrosion products, so it may help other microbes speed up the decay.
events.why: Corrosion is not only chemistry: living things can speed it up in the deep sea.

events.title: The IMPACT study puts a global price on corrosion
events.text: NACE International's IMPACT study estimated the global cost of corrosion at about US$2.5 trillion a year, roughly 3.4 percent of global GDP. It was built on national studies and extrapolated, so it is a rough guide, not an exact number.
events.why: It is the best-known single figure for what rust and other corrosion cost the world.

facts: The Delhi iron pillar has stood about 1,600 years, and its rust formed fast in the first three years then nearly stopped.
The Eiffel Tower's paint layers add up to about 3 millimetres after 19 repaintings.
Davy found a small area of iron was enough to keep a large area of copper clean: about 1 part to 150.
The first true stainless steel had 12.8 percent chromium.
A rust-eating bacterium was named from a rusticle on the Titanic, 3.8 kilometres down.
